title: Integration of camera traps with direct observation surveys in monitoring of birds under unequal temporal coverage
content:
Our study compares motion-activated camera traps with conventional direct observation using 6 years of bird-monitoring data from Jeju Island. Camera traps recorded additional species and revealed detection biases linked to camera height and bird-to-camera distance, complementing observer-based surveys. Together, these findings show how integrating the two methods improves completeness and supports more consistent, effort-standardised biodiversity indicators.


Abstract

Camera traps (CT) are increasingly recognised as efficient tools for biodiversity monitoring, but their methodological performance in bird community research remains poorly understood. We evaluated the complementarity between CT and conventional direct observation (DO) surveys using a 6-year dataset (2018–2023) from one montane wetland on Jeju Island and four nearby islets in the Republic of Korea. Across the five sites, 30 CT generated 18,780 camera-station days. We examined shared and method-specific detections between CT and DO under unequal temporal coverage, diel community structure using CT records, seasonal method-specific richness accumulation using rarefaction, and the influence of camera-station configuration and bird-to-camera detection distance on CT-based richness estimates. CT recorded 65 species and DO recorded 85, with 41 species shared, 44 unique to DO, and 24 unique to CT, increasing total species richness to 109. McNemar's test confirmed a significant detection imbalance (χ 2 = 5.31, p = 0.021), and diel analyses indicated modest but significant community turnover (R 2 = 0.0061, p < 0.01). Seasonal rarefaction showed similar richness estimates for CT and DO in spring and summer, whereas DO recorded higher richness in autumn and winter. Branch-mounted cameras recorded the highest mean daily richness, with significantly lower values at ground and water stations, whereas flight stations did not differ significantly from branch stations. Species richness per unit area declined with increasing bird-to-camera distance. Practical implication. CT complements DO by expanding temporal coverage and detecting species overlooked during observer-based surveys. Integrating camera placement, effort-standardised metrics, and distance-aware modelling provides a transferable framework for incorporating CT into long-term avian monitoring programmes and improving detectability-based biodiversity indicators under field conditions.
